title: Pandu's message
hookLine: a father among the dead asks his son for a deed; why Hindus still make offerings for their ancestors
carry: what we do still reaches the ancestors

cards: Yudhishthira has been listening closely, and he's noticed something. In Indra's hall, among all the sages and gods, Narada named only one human king: Harishchandra.
Not the great kings of Yudhishthira's own line, not the heroes of the old stories. One name. Why him? the king asks.
And there's a second question underneath. In Yama's hall, among the dead, you saw my father. You saw Pandu.

teach.b: Narada answers the first question first. Harishchandra was a mighty king who brought other kings under him and then performed the great sacrifice called the Rajasuya.

He gave generously to everyone who came, and because of that sacrifice, he shines in Indra's hall. Then the second answer. Narada had seen Pandu in Yama's hall, and Pandu had seen Harishchandra's place.
So Pandu gave Narada a message. Tell my son: you are able to conquer the earth, and your brothers obey you.

teach.h: TELL MY SON: PERFORM THE RAJASUYA.
teach.b: Perform the Rajasuya. Then I, and our ancestors, may go to Indra's world. Sit with that.

Yudhishthira's father died when the brothers were young, and now, in the brand-new hall, a sage delivers his words. Not comfort. A request, and a heavy one: do this, so that I, and the fathers before me, can rise.
That isn't only Pandu's wish. It's one of Hinduism's oldest ideas.

teach.h: THE PITRIS, STILL TIED TO US.
teach.b: The living and the ancestors, the pitris, stay tied together, and what the living do can still reach them.
Old Vedic texts say every person is born owing three debts: to the gods, to the sages who taught, and to the ancestors.

That last debt is paid by carrying the family on, and by honoring the dead in shraddha: offerings of rice, sesame and water, made for the dead by name, often by a son, just as Pandu turns to his eldest.
Every year, in the fortnight called Pitru Paksha, many Hindu families do it together.
Many teachers read it simply: love doesn't stop at death. Tomorrow, Narada adds something far less welcome.

how: Hindu families honor their ancestors in shraddha rites, with offerings of rice (pinda), sesame and water, and in Pitru Paksha, the fortnight when the ancestors are remembered together.

o: a hall, and the assembly gathered in it
the world where kings go after they die
a message carried by a wandering sage

games.q: a father's message, and the ancestors — tap the pairs.
p: seen by Narada in Yama's hall
the ancestors, still tied to the living
offerings made for the dead by name

s: Pandu appeared to Yudhishthira in a dream
the message came through Narada, a guest in the sabha.
in Hindu belief, what the living do can still reach the ancestors
that is why families keep shraddha and Pitru Paksha for the pitris.
Pandu asked only for his son's happiness
he asked him to perform the Rajasuya, so that he and the ancestors could go to Indra's world.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. your father, among the dead, asks through Narada for a deed that will lift him and the ancestors. how do you hear it?
o: as a ghost story; the dead are gone.
as a real tie: what i do can still reach them.
as an order to obey without a second thought.
games.why: he takes it to heart, and so does the tradition: shraddha rests on the same tie between the living and the pitris. still, tomorrow he weighs it carefully before he acts.

practice: If your family keeps Pitru Paksha or shraddha, this is a small version of it.

Pour a little water into a cup or onto a plant, and as you pour, say the name of someone in your family who has died, a grandparent or someone further back, and thank them for one thing that reached you.
If you pray, offer the water to them and to God. If you don't, just say the name and the thank you, and let the water go.

wordCard.voice: Sabha. A hall, and its assembly. Today, in Yudhishthira's sabha, a sage carries a message from his father among the dead.

orig.note: Sanskrit hariścandra: the king Narada names in Indra's hall, there because of his Rajasuya.

carryVoice: Your line: what we do still reaches the ancestors. Pandu asked his son, and Hindu families still answer with water and rice. Day seven hundred fifty.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Lokapala Sabhakhyana Parva (Yudhishthira asks about Harishchandra and Pandu; Narada delivers Pandu's message)
Taittiriya Samhita 6.3.10 (a person is born owing three debts: to the sages, the gods and the ancestors)
